layer-oud-with-body-butter.before:
Oud is one of the richest notes in perfumery: smoky, resinous and warm. Yet even a great oud perfume can fade sooner than you expect on dry skin. The fix is simple and costs very little: layer it over a body butter. Here is why it works, how to do it, and three pairings from our shelves to try.

Why fragrance lasts longer on moisturised skin

Perfume oils evaporate fastest from dry skin. A thin layer of butter or lotion gives the fragrance something to cling to, so it tends to unfold more slowly and stay closer to you for longer. Rich butters with cocoa, shea or almond oil work especially well under warm notes such as oud, amber and vanilla. If your skin runs dry, a body butter for dry skin does two jobs at once.

How to layer, step by step

  1. Shower first. Pat skin almost dry; slightly damp skin takes butter more evenly.
  2. Warm a little butter between your palms and press it into pulse points: wrists, inner elbows, the base of the neck and behind the knees.
  3. Wait a minute so the butter settles.
  4. Spray once or twice from about 15 cm onto the same spots. Don't rub your wrists together; let it dry.
  5. Top up the butter, not the perfume, later in the day if skin feels dry. The scent often comes back with it.

Three skin + scent pairings to try

1. Sweet and golden: Chocolate Body Butter + Amber Oud Gold

The Deyga Chocolate Body Butter is made with cocoa and nourishing oils and has a light chocolate scent. Under Al Haramain Amber Oud Gold Edition, with its melon, pineapple, vanilla and musk, it reads as a soft gourmand. For more intensity, try the Amber Oud Extreme Gold Edition extrait. "Chocolate body butter" and "Al Haramain Amber Oud" are both popular UK searches, and this is the pairing that shows why.

2. Floral and warm: Rose & Geranium Body Butter + Amber Oud Ruby

The Deyga Rose & Geranium Body Butter carries rose and geranium essential oils. Layer it under Al Haramain Amber Oud Ruby Edition, which opens with saffron and bitter almond over jasmine, cedarwood, ambergris and musk, and the florals meet in the middle. If you love rose with oud, Montale Aoud Damascus is another lovely match.

3. Clean and smoky: a light lotion + Gucci Intense Oud

Not every pairing needs a scented base. A light, quick-absorbing lotion such as Vilvah Milk Body Lotion lets a dark scent like Gucci Intense Oud (black pepper, incense, woods, leather and an oud accord) lead the way, while still giving it something to hold on to. Want a luxury option? Try Highborn London Natural Luminosity Body Butter.

Which base suits your skin?

If your skin is very dry, a rich butter such as Deyga's cocoa or rose formulas gives the most staying power. If you prefer something lighter in warm weather, a lotion like Deyga Almond Milk Body Lotion absorbs faster and still helps the fragrance last. On sensitive days, keep the base unscented and let the perfume do the talking.

A few tips for oud

  • Less is more. Oud projects well; one or two sprays over butter usually lasts.
  • Spray clothes lightly, not silk, to keep a soft trail.
  • Match the mood. Sweet butters suit amber ouds, floral butters suit rose ouds, and neutral lotions suit smoky ouds.

New to oud and Arabian perfume? Our guide to Lattafa Khamrah Qahwa and Arabian perfume explains the notes and how to choose.

lattafa-khamrah-qahwa-arabian-perfume.before:
Few perfumes have travelled by word of mouth like Lattafa Khamrah Qahwa. It belongs to a wave of Arabian perfume houses, from Lattafa and Afnan to Al Haramain, Arabiyat Prestige and Maison Alhambra, whose rich, warm scents have found a big following in the UK. Here is what is in Khamrah Qahwa, what makes a perfume "Arabian", and how to choose one.

What does Lattafa Khamrah Qahwa smell like?

"Qahwa" is the Arabic word for coffee, and that is the idea at the heart of Lattafa Khamrah Qahwa Eau de Parfum (£26.99, 100ml). Its notes, from top to base:

  • Top: cinnamon, cardamom and ginger, the spices of Arabic coffee.
  • Heart: praline, candied fruits and white flowers.
  • Base: coffee, vanilla, tonka bean, benzoin and musk.

So it opens spicy, turns sweet and nutty, and settles into coffee and vanilla. It is an amber-woody, gourmand scent made for men and women, and it suits cooler months and evenings best.

More from Lattafa

Lattafa perfume is known for warm, generous scents at friendly prices. Alongside Khamrah Qahwa, we list:

  • Lattafa Teriaq (£29.99): caramel, bitter almond, pink pepper and apricot, then honey, rhubarb and rose over leather, vanilla and musk. Unisex.
  • Lattafa Maahir Black Edition (£25.99): black and pink pepper with saffron, then labdanum and cade oil over leather, cedarwood, guaiac wood and patchouli. A darker, smoky choice.
  • Lattafa Yara Candy (£26.99): green mandarin and blackcurrant, a strawberry-candy and gardenia heart, and vanilla, musk and sandalwood. Made for women.

See every Lattafa scent on the Lattafa page.

Afnan, Arabiyat Prestige and Maison Alhambra

Afnan 9am Dive (£26.99) is the fresh one: lemon, mint, pink pepper and blackcurrant, then apple, incense and cedarwood. Afnan Supremacy Gold (£27.99) is warmer, with nutmeg, violet and peach blossom over amber, vanilla, oud and benzoin. More on the Afnan page.

Arabiyat Prestige Nyla (£25.99, 80ml) is a bright floral-fruity scent for women: coconut, peach and mandarin, then tiare, jasmine and rose over white musk. See Arabiyat Prestige. Maison Alhambra adds a wide range of floral, fruity and woody eau de parfums at friendly prices.

What makes a perfume "Arabian"?

There is no strict rule, but Arabian perfume usually leans on a few ingredients:

  • Oud (agarwood): a deep, woody, slightly smoky note.
  • Amber and resins such as benzoin and labdanum: warm and sweet.
  • Saffron, cardamom and cinnamon: spice.
  • Rose and musk: soft and rounded.

Most of the scents above are eau de parfum, which typically holds around 15–20% perfume oil. Read extrait vs eau de parfum for what each label means.

Arabian perfume in stock now

Warm and spicy

Al Haramain Amber Oud Tobacco Edition (£32.99, 60ml) shares Khamrah Qahwa's love of spice: tobacco leaf, cinnamon, black pepper and ginger, then vanilla, clove, star anise, cacao and tonka bean. Al Haramain Amber Oud Black Edition (£39.99) pairs cardamom and lavender with leather, amber and benzoin.

Sweet and fruity

Al Haramain Amber Oud Gold Edition (from £32.99) is bergamot, melon and pineapple over vanilla and musk, a popular first Arabian perfume. Al Haramain Amber Oud Ruby Edition (from £41.99) mixes saffron and bitter almond with jasmine and ambergris. Al Haramain Amber Musk (£39.99) is softer: amber, musk, vanilla and resins.

Oud and saffron

Fumeri Oud Saffron (£29.99) and SAP Saffron Oud Extrait de Parfum (£43.99) both open on saffron and spice before oud, cedarwood and smoky woods, with amber, leather and musk. Montale Aoud Safran (£62.99) builds on saffron and oud with rose and amber.

Browse all Arabian perfume and oud perfume.

How to wear a rich, warm perfume

  • Start small: one or two sprays on the neck or wrists. You can add more; you cannot take it away.
  • Spray on moisturised skin, so the scent has something to sit on. We explain how in how to layer oud with body butter.
  • Try it on skin before you decide. Warm notes change over the first hour, so judge the base, not just the first spray.
  • Patch test if your skin is sensitive to fragrance.

moisturiser-for-your-skin-type.before:
A good moisturiser is the step that holds the rest of your routine together. It softens skin, helps it feel comfortable all day and gives make-up or sunscreen a smooth base. But the right texture depends on your skin: a rich cream that rescues dry skin can feel heavy on oily skin, and a light lotion may not be enough in winter. Here is how to choose a moisturiser for your skin type.

Cream, lotion or gel: what is the difference?

Most moisturisers mix water with oils and butters. The more oil and butter, the richer the texture:

  • Rich creams hold more butters and oils, such as shea butter and almond oil. They suit dry and very dry skin, and cold weather.
  • Light creams and lotions have more water and lighter oils. They suit normal, oily and combination skin.
  • Gels and serums are mostly water with moisture-loving ingredients such as glycerine and hyaluronic acid. They work on their own for oily skin, or under a cream.

Moisturiser for dry skin

Dry skin feels tight, may flake and drinks a light lotion straight in. Look for a cream with butters and oils.

Deyga Deep Moisturising Face Cream (£18.99, 30g) blends shea butter with marula and almond oils, centella asiatica (gotu kola) and cardamom, and Deyga makes it without artificial fragrance. Highborn London Imperial Moisturiser (£46, 50ml) is a richer, nourishing cream made in England for dry, tight-feeling skin. See more moisturisers for dry skin.

Moisturiser for oily skin

Oily skin still needs moisture: skipping it can leave skin feeling tight while it still looks shiny. Choose a light, fast-absorbing texture.

Deyga Light Moisturising Face Cream (£18.99, 30g) is made for oily and normal skin, with rosehip, almond and avocado oils, shea butter, centella asiatica and ectoin, and a hint of vanilla essential oil. On very oily days, a serum such as Deyga 2% Hyaluronic Acid Serum (£22.99, 20ml) can be enough on its own. More ideas for oily skin.

Moisturiser for sensitive skin

Sensitive skin does best with a short ingredient list and no added fragrance. Of the creams above, the Deyga Deep Moisturising Face Cream is made without artificial fragrance; the Light cream contains vanilla essential oil, so patch test it first. Introduce one new product at a time, and see more for sensitive skin.

Moisturiser for combination skin

Combination skin is oily through the centre and normal or dry on the cheeks. Use a light moisturiser all over and add a little richer cream only where skin feels dry. Vilvah Ultra Moisturising Cream (£25.99, 50ml) is a good middle ground: olive squalane, glycerine and plant extracts in a non-greasy cream that Vilvah makes for all skin types, with white lily essential oil.

Add a hydrating serum underneath

Serums are light and watery, so they go on before your moisturiser. A hyaluronic acid serum such as the Deyga 2% Hyaluronic Acid Serum (sodium hyaluronate, panthenol, aloe and centella) or Vilvah Milk Drops Hydrating Serum (from £21.99), with aloe vera juice, hyaluronic acid and rice milk extract, adds a layer of moisture that the cream then seals in. Aloe vera gel works in a similar way; read how to use aloe vera gel. Browse every serum.

Day cream or night cream?

By day, your moisturiser sits under sunscreen and make-up, so a lighter texture often works best. Finish with SPF, or use a moisturiser with SPF built in, such as Highborn London GLOWGUARD SPF30 Moisturiser (from £49), which uses non-nano zinc oxide.

At night there is no sunscreen or make-up to layer, so many people like something richer. A night cream such as Highborn London Night Elixir (from £26) is a comforting cream made for the last step of an evening routine. The Ultimate Day & Night Moisture Set (£95) pairs it with the Imperial Moisturiser.

How to apply moisturiser

  1. Cleanse with a face wash that suits your skin: see face wash for your skin type.
  2. Apply serum, if you use one, to slightly damp skin.
  3. Warm a pea-sized amount of moisturiser between your fingertips.
  4. Press and smooth it over your face and neck with upward strokes, avoiding the eyes.
  5. In the morning, finish with sunscreen unless your moisturiser has SPF.

What makes a moisturiser "natural"?

There is no legal definition of "natural" in the UK, so read the ingredient list rather than the label. In the creams above you will find plant butters and oils (shea, marula, rosehip, avocado, almond, olive squalane) alongside glycerine, water and an emulsifier that keeps them blended. Full ingredient lists are on every product page.

Good to know

  • Patch test a new moisturiser on your jaw or inner arm for 24 hours.
  • Your skin changes with the seasons: many people switch to a richer cream in winter and a lighter one in summer.
  • Dryness, redness or itching that lasts is worth showing to a pharmacist or your GP.

face-mask-guide.before:
A face mask is the easiest way to give your skin ten minutes of extra care. Once or twice a week, it can leave skin feeling fresher, softer or more comfortable, depending on the type you choose. Here are the main kinds of face mask, which suits your skin, and how to use one.

The main types of face mask

  • Clay masks use clays such as kaolin or French pink clay. They dry down on the skin and feel deep-cleansing, which makes them popular with oily and combination skin.
  • Charcoal masks add activated charcoal, often with tea tree, for a fresh, clarifying feel.
  • Powder face packs are dry blends of plant powders that you mix with water, rose water or aloe gel just before use.
  • Cream and gel masks are hydrating and stay soft on the skin, which suits dry and tired-looking skin.

Clay face masks

Vilvah Milk Mud Mask (£19.99, 50ml) is a creamy clay face mask: kaolin clay with oat milk extract, saffron extract and liquorice root extract, made without sulphates, silicones or artificial fragrance, and suitable for all skin types including sensitive skin. Vilvah Wild Rose Face Mask (£11.99, 100ml) keeps things short and simple: aloe vera, French pink clay and rose hydrosol. Vilvah suggests using it two or three times a week.

Charcoal face masks

Deyga Charcoal Detox Face Mask (£13.99, 100g) combines activated charcoal with tea tree and jasmine hydrosols, and is made without parabens or artificial fragrance. Vilvah Charcoal Face Mask (£12.99, 100ml) pairs charcoal with aloe vera and tea tree hydrosol. Both have a fresh, clean feel that many people with oily skin enjoy. See more face masks for oily skin.

Powder face packs

Face packs are a long-standing part of Indian skincare: dried herbs, fruit peels and clays ground to a powder and mixed fresh each time.

  • Deyga Orange & Almond Face Pack (£19.99, 100g): sun-dried orange pulp and zest, almond meal and turmeric. The almond meal gives it a gentle, polishing texture.
  • Deyga Spirulina Matcha Face Pack (£17.99, 150g): spirulina, matcha, neem, moringa and aloe vera powder, for a green, earthy mask.

Mix a teaspoon with water, or with Deyga Pure Rose Water Toner (£11.99) for a softer scent, into a smooth paste. You may know the classic Indian clay multani mitti (Fuller's earth) used the same way; kaolin and French pink clay are other clays used in face masks.

Hydrating masks and eye masks

For skin that feels dry or tired rather than oily, choose a cream or gel mask that stays soft. The 24K Gold Hydrating Face Mask (£34.99) combines 24K gold with hyaluronic acid, ceramides, shea butter and centella asiatica, and makes a lovely treat or gift. For the delicate eye area, Deyga Under Eye Mask (£15.99, 15g) is a balm of kalonji, hemp seed, almond, rosehip and carrot seed oils with beeswax, to dab on at night.

Which face mask suits your skin?

  • Oily or combination skin: clay or charcoal masks, on the T-zone or the whole face.
  • Dry skin: a hydrating cream mask, or a creamy clay mask such as the Milk Mud Mask, rinsed off before it dries completely.
  • Sensitive skin: a short ingredient list without added fragrance, and a patch test first.
  • Not sure? Try multi-masking: clay on the oily areas, a hydrating mask on the dry ones.

How to use a face mask

  1. Cleanse first with a face wash that suits your skin: see face wash for your skin type.
  2. Apply an even layer with clean fingertips or a brush, avoiding the eyes and lips.
  3. Leave it on for the time on the pack, usually 10 to 15 minutes. Rinse clay masks before they crack and pull, so skin does not feel tight.
  4. Rinse with lukewarm water and a soft cloth, then pat dry.
  5. Follow with toner and moisturiser straight away. Aloe vera gel is a light option: read how to use aloe vera gel.

How often should you use a face mask?

For most people, clay and charcoal masks once or twice a week are plenty; dry or sensitive skin may prefer once a week. Hydrating masks can be used more often. Always follow the directions on the pack.

Good to know

  • Patch test any new mask on your jaw or inner arm first.
  • Turmeric can leave a faint yellow tint on skin and towels; rinse well and use an old towel.
  • Skip masks on broken, sunburnt or irritated skin. Breakouts or redness that last are worth showing to a pharmacist or your GP.
